title: The first week
hookLine: sin and mercy, ending in a conversation at the foot of the cross
carry: what have I done for christ

lines: GO TO THE FOOT OF THE CROSS.
cards: The first week of the Exercises is not gentle. Ignatius asks the person praying to look at sin, the world's and then their own, plainly, without excuses. Things said that can't be unsaid.
It would be easy to get stuck there, in a pile of regret. He doesn't let it end there. At the close of the hour he moves the person to the foot of the cross, face to face, and talking.
Not reciting. Talking. Today's word is the name he gives that talk.

teach.h: AS ONE FRIEND SPEAKS TO ANOTHER.
teach.b: Ignatius says to make it the way one friend speaks to another, or the way a servant speaks to a master: asking for something, admitting something, saying what's on your mind and asking advice.
Imagine Christ our Lord in front of you, hanging on the cross. Ask how it is that the Creator became human, and went from eternal life to death, for my sins.
Then turn to yourself with three questions. What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ?
What ought I to do for Christ? The week began with sin, and sin can turn a person inward, into shame. The colloquy turns them outward, toward a face.
The questions are not a scorecard. They come after time spent looking at someone who loved first.
Saint Paul has a line in Galatians that fits, in the Douay-Rheims: the Son of God, "who loved me, and delivered himself for me." Me, singular.
Ignatius also asks the one praying to wonder that they've been allowed to go on living, that the earth has held them up, that mercy kept the door open.
So the first week runs sin, then mercy, then conversation.

teach.h: WHO LOVED ME, AND DELIVERED HIMSELF FOR ME.
teach.b: Ignatius closes the colloquy with an Our Father, but the talk before it belongs to the one praying. Guilt alone tends to spin in place. A conversation goes somewhere.

how: In the first week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray over sin and God's mercy, and end each prayer time with a colloquy, an unscripted conversation with Christ, often closed with the Our Father.

o: a formal prayer recited word for word
a heart-to-heart talk with Christ in prayer
a group discussion led by a retreat director

games.q: the first week — tap the pairs.

s: the first week ends with the person stuck in their sins
it ends in a conversation with Christ on the cross.
Ignatius writes out the words of the colloquy for you
he gives the setting and the questions. the talk is the person's own, closed with an Our Father.
the three questions ask what I have done, am doing and ought to do for Christ
past, present, and the next step.

games.q: you've spent an hour looking honestly at your own failures. the Exercises say: now what?
o: keep listing them until you've found every one.
turn to Christ on the cross and talk, as to a friend.
put it away and think about something cheerful.
games.why: Ignatius closes the meditation with a colloquy: a face, three questions, and an Our Father. sin is looked at, then mercy, then talk.

practice: If there's a crucifix nearby, look at it; if not, let the image come to mind.
If you pray, speak to Christ in your own words, the way you'd talk to a friend at a hospital bedside, then let the first question sit: what have I done for Christ?
If you don't pray, stay with the image of someone who gave something up for you, and ask what you've done in return.

wordCard.voice: Colloquy. A conversation, as one friend speaks to another, here at the foot of the cross. This week ran from Dominic's last promise to his brothers into the first week of Ignatius's Exercises. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, the word Ignatius uses in the Exercises: a conversation, a talk between two.

carryVoice: Your line: what have I done for Christ. The other two questions follow: what am I doing, and what ought I to do. Until tomorrow.
